children: By Staff Writer

The proposed Dangote-backed refinery in Kenya’s Lamu is moving ahead of Uganda’s long-delayed 60,000-barrels-per-day refinery at Hoima, with officials of the Nigerian conglomerate reportedly targeting the end of September for groundbreaking and immediate construction of the multibillion-dollar project.

If the schedule holds, the 700,000-barrels-per-day Lamu refinery could be commissioned in 2030, giving it a potentially decisive headstart over Uganda’s Kabaale refinery, whose final investment decision (FID) has been pushed to the first quarter of 2027.

Uganda National Oil Company (Unoc) spokesperson Tony Otoa said the FID remains contingent on completion of Front-End Engineering Design (FEED) studies, early works, technical milestones, commercial agreements and regulatory approvals.“FEED studies are progressing on schedule, alongside ongoing preparations for early works activities,” Mr Otoa said, adding that their completion will inform the developers’ final investment decision.
The FEED programme covers basic engineering, topographical and geotechnical surveys, logistics studies, project execution planning and the Environmental and Social Impact Assessment.
The Kabaale refinery is estimated to cost about $4 billion.
The widening gap between the two projects matters because they are entering a global oil market that is changing rapidly.

Electric vehicles are already eating into demand for petrol and diesel, particularly in China, the world’s second-largest oil consumer. In the first half of 2026 alone, EVs—including electric trucks—were estimated to have displaced about 36 million tonnes of oil demand in China.“The energy industry is developing very, very fast. These refineries are up against EVs. They can’t afford any delays. Uganda’s oil project has taken too long to start,” said Dr John Mutenyo, an energy economist and senior lecturer at Makerere University.

For Uganda, the concern is not only the timing of the refinery but the timing of the wider oil project. The country discovered about 6.5 billion barrels of commercially viable oil resources between 2006 and 2014 but, nearly two decades later, is only now approaching first commercial production and crude exports.

Uganda expects first crude exports in the first quarter of 2027, with the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (Eacop) nearing completion to transport crude from the Albertine Graben to Tanzania’s port of Tanga.

But by the time Kabaale and Lamu are fully operational, refiners could be competing in a market increasingly shaped by electrification, decarbonisation and weaker petroleum demand in major economies.“The earlier you do it, the better,” Dr Mutenyo said, arguing that delays expose Uganda’s oil industry to a rapidly changing market.

He said environmental pressure to reduce fossil-fuel consumption, the global push towards electric vehicles and geopolitical efforts to reduce dependence on Russian oil following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine are all reshaping long-term petroleum demand.
Dangote Group is targeting about 30 months for construction of the Lamu facility. If work begins this month, the refinery could be ready around early 2029.
Kabaale, by contrast, has yet to secure a construction start date. Even with a similar construction period, it could come online in the second half of 2030.
The difference may be little more than a year, but in a capital-intensive industry, that can be significant.

Lamu is being positioned to serve northern Kenya, Somalia, South Sudan and Ethiopia, potentially putting it in a strong position to supply regional markets—including the Mombasa-Kampala corridor—before Uganda’s refinery begins producing.
Kabaale, meanwhile, is primarily designed to meet Uganda’s domestic fuel needs while supplying neighbouring markets.
That gives Lamu a potential first-mover advantage in a region where fuel demand is still growing, even as the long-term global outlook for petroleum becomes less certain.

Uganda’s strategy is therefore based less on competing head-on with coastal refineries and more on using its inland location and domestic crude supply to reduce dependence on imported refined products.
President Yoweri Museveni has maintained that the Kabaale refinery remains a strategic priority despite the development of Eacop and plans to export crude through Tanzania.

The economic argument is straightforward: refining crude inland could reduce Uganda’s exposure to the cost of importing refined petroleum and transporting it from the coast.“Our refinery will be one of the most profitable because, first of all, it’s far from the ocean and it does not have the transportation cost which imported oil has,” Mr Museveni recently said.

He cited the $12.77-per-barrel cost of transporting Uganda’s crude to Tanga as an example of the savings that could potentially be achieved by refining domestically.“When we refine our oil here, we don’t pay that money. We shall no longer spend $2 billion importing petroleum,” he said, adding that while some crude could be exported, the refinery would receive priority under Uganda’s agreements.

The government’s argument is strengthened by the fact that Uganda currently imports virtually all of its petroleum products, leaving the country exposed to international prices, shipping costs and regional supply disruptions.
But getting Kabaale to this point has taken years.
Uganda initially selected Russia’s RT Global Resources in 2015 as the preferred bidder to build the refinery. The consortium withdrew in 2016 after negotiations stalled.
South Korea’s SK Engineering was subsequently brought into the project but also exited after declining to assume the financing risk associated with its proposed 60 percent stake.

In 2018, Kampala selected the Albertine Graben Energy Consortium, comprising US and Italian firms, as its private-sector partner. That project framework agreement eventually lapsed in June 2023 after the government said the consortium had failed to meet key milestones, particularly on financing.
The latest attempt began in March 2025, when Uganda signed an implementation agreement with UAE-based MBM Alpha Investments LLC, with Alpha MBM taking a 60 percent stake and Unoc 40 percent.
The refinery is expected to produce LPG, petrol, diesel, kerosene and jet fuel for Uganda and regional markets.

Unoc had previously projected an FID in 2026, construction thereafter and commissioning in 2029 or 2030. The latest shift of the FID to early 2027 has now pushed the project further into the period when global petroleum demand is expected to face greater structural pressure.
Regional energy leaders see the emergence of both projects as potentially positive for East Africa, which still relies heavily on imported refined petroleum products despite producing crude oil.
But the bigger question is whether Lamu and Kabaale can operate as complementary regional assets rather than competing national projects.

African Energy Chamber Executive Chairman NJ Ayuk cautioned against turning the two refineries into national prestige projects without sufficient attention to financing, feedstock, infrastructure and regional coordination.“If executed with discipline, they can complement each other, serve a rapidly growing East African market, create thousands of jobs and retain billions of dollars within Africa,” he said.
That regional approach could become critical as both projects move closer to reality.

In April, Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote announced at an infrastructure summit in Nairobi that his group planned to build a replica of its 700,000-barrels-per-day Lekki refinery in Nigeria, signalling the scale of its ambitions for East Africa.

For Uganda, the challenge is now clear: after years of delays and failed partnerships, Kabaale must move from engineering studies to construction while the market it was designed to serve is itself undergoing a fundamental transformation.

The issue is no longer simply whether Uganda can build a refinery. It is whether it can build one quickly enough—and at the right scale—to remain commercially relevant in a market that is steadily moving beyond oil.
